Replacing existing debt with new debt, usually to get a lower interest rate, longer maturity, looser terms or extra borrowing.
The risk that a borrower cannot replace maturing debt, or can do so only at much higher cost or tighter terms.
Release of blocked money for shares not allotted.
The firm that processes IPO applications, decides allotment under SEBI rules and handles refunds.
The straight line that best fits a scatter of points. The slope is how much Y changes for each 1-unit rise in X; the intercept is the value of Y where the line crosses X = 0.
terms.formula: Y = Intercept + Slope × X

terms.meaning: The version of a mutual fund bought through a distributor or advisor. A commission for them is paid out of the fund, so its yearly cost is higher than the Direct plan's.
A disclosure made under Regulation 30 of SEBI's listing rules (LODR), which requires companies to report material events promptly.
Putting income from an investment, such as dividends or interest, back into the same or another investment instead of withdrawing it.
The share of after-tax operating profit a company puts back into the business through net capex and working capital.
terms.formula: (Net capex + Increase in working capital) ÷ NOPAT

terms.meaning: Disclosure in the notes of transactions and balances with related parties, such as promoters, subsidiaries, associates, directors and their relatives, required under Ind AS 24.
A deal between a company and parties connected to it, such as promoters, directors, their relatives, or group companies.
A share's return minus the return of an index over the same period, in percentage points. Positive means the share did better than the index. It is different from RSI.
terms.formula: Relative return = Share's return − Index return

terms.meaning: Comparing a company's valuation ratio with its own past (for example its 5-year median P/E) or with the median of its sector.
Converting electronic shares in a demat account back into physical share certificates, through a request to the depository participant.
Valuing a company or asset at what it would cost today to rebuild or replace its assets with similar ones.
The policy rate at which the central bank lends short-term funds to banks against eligible collateral.
A short-term borrowing deal in which one party transfers securities to another for cash and agrees to repurchase them later at a slightly higher price.
A floating lending rate directly linked to the RBI's repo rate plus a spread, a common form of external benchmark lending rate.
terms.formula: Repo rate + Spread

terms.meaning: Statements of fact made by the seller in a purchase agreement about the company, such as its accounts, taxes, contracts and legal compliance; if untrue, the acquirer can claim compensation.
Money spent on research into new products or processes and on developing them. Research costs are expensed; development costs can be capitalised when strict conditions are met.
terms.formula: R&D intensity = R&D expense ÷ Revenue

terms.meaning: The portion of a fund's capital set aside for follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies rather than new deals.
A list of key decisions in a shareholders' agreement that need specific investor approval, such as changing the business, issuing shares or approving budgets.
The part of shareholders' equity other than share capital, made up mainly of accumulated retained profits, securities premium and other reserves. Under Ind AS it is shown within Other Equity.
Valuing equity as current book value plus the present value of future residual income, that is, profits above the cost of equity.
terms.formula: Book value + Present value of (Net profit − Cost of equity × Opening book value)

terms.meaning: The ratio of the current net asset value of a fund's unrealised investments to the total capital limited partners have contributed.
terms.formula: Residual NAV ÷ Paid-in capital

terms.meaning: Cash a company cannot freely use for operations because it is set aside for a specific purpose, such as unpaid dividend accounts, margin money with banks or debt service reserves.
A loan whose terms, such as repayment schedule, interest rate or tenure, have been changed to help a struggling borrower keep repaying.

FinLit's plain reading of a quarterly result. Revenue growth, profit growth and the change in margin on a year ago are each compared with the typical company in the same NSE industry. Above on most of them: Strong or Good. Below on most: Weak or Poor.

The results season is the few weeks after each quarter ends, when most listed companies report. The results calendar lists the board-meeting dates companies have announced for approving their results.
Individuals and other non-institutional holders, grouped as 'public' in the shareholding pattern.
An individual who invests personal money in shares, bonds or funds, as opposed to an institution. In Indian IPOs, a retail individual investor is one applying for up to ₹2 lakh.
Profit a company has kept over the years instead of paying it out as dividends.
terms.formula: Retained earnings = Opening balance + Net income − Dividends

terms.meaning: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
terms.formula: Retention ratio % = 100 − Payout ratio %

terms.meaning: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
terms.formula: ROA % = Net profit ÷ Total assets × 100

terms.meaning: EBIT divided by capital employed; it measures operating return on long-term capital.
terms.formula: ROCE % = EBIT ÷ (Shareholders' equity + Debt) × 100

terms.meaning: Profit after tax divided by average shareholders' equity; it measures profit generated from owners' funds.
terms.formula: ROE % = Net profit ÷ Average shareholders' equity × 100

terms.meaning: Breaking return on equity into three parts: net profit margin, asset turnover and financial leverage (equity multiplier).
terms.formula: ROE = (Net profit ÷ Revenue) × (Revenue ÷ Total assets) × (Total assets ÷ Shareholders' equity)

terms.meaning: After-tax operating profit as a percentage of the capital invested in the business by both shareholders and lenders.
terms.formula: NOPAT ÷ Invested capital × 100

terms.meaning: The gain or loss on an investment as a share of what it cost.
terms.formula: ROI % = Net gain ÷ Cost of investment × 100

terms.meaning: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
terms.formula: Return on tangible assets % = Net profit ÷ (Total assets − Intangible assets) × 100

terms.meaning: The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before any costs are taken out. Also called sales, turnover or the 'top line'.
The percentage of recurring revenue lost in a period through cancellations and downgrades, before counting expansion revenue from existing customers.
terms.formula: Recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades ÷ Recurring revenue at start of period × 100

terms.meaning: How much of a company's revenue depends on a few customers, products, segments or regions.
terms.formula: Revenue from largest source ÷ Total revenue × 100

terms.meaning: The Ind AS 115 framework requiring revenue to be recognised in five steps: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, set the price, allocate it, and recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.
A valuation multiple comparing a company's value, usually enterprise value or market cap, with its revenue.
terms.formula: Enterprise value (or Market cap) ÷ Revenue

terms.meaning: The accounting rules that determine when and how much revenue a company records, generally when control of goods or services passes to the customer, as set out in Ind AS 115.
How confidently a company's future revenue can be predicted from existing orders, contracts or recurring customers.
Funding in which investors provide capital in return for a fixed share of future revenue until a set total, usually a multiple of the amount advanced, is repaid.
A DCF run backwards: it starts from today's share price and works out the growth that price implies.
The interest rate at which the RBI borrows money from banks against government securities, used to absorb surplus liquidity.
The other side of a repo: a party lends cash by acquiring securities and agrees to return them later at a higher price.

A corporate action that combines several existing shares into one share of higher face value, cutting the share count and raising the price per share proportionally without changing the company's total value.
An arrangement in which founders receive all their shares upfront, but the company can repurchase unvested shares at a nominal price if a founder leaves before a set period.
A revolving credit facility that a company can draw, repay and redraw up to a set limit, used for working capital and short-term needs.
A committed borrowing limit that a company can draw, repay and draw again during the agreed period, up to a maximum amount.
The updated offer document filed before the IPO opens, with almost everything except the final price and number of shares.
A right requiring a shareholder who wants to transfer shares to first offer them to specified parties, who can make an offer before the shares are offered to outsiders.
A right for the company or existing investors to match a third party's offer for shares before a shareholder can transfer them to that outsider.
An asset recorded by a lessee representing its right to use a leased item, such as a building or aircraft, over the lease term, initially measured at the lease liability plus related costs.
terms.formula: Lease liability + Initial direct costs + Prepaid lease payments − Incentives received

terms.meaning: The right given to existing shareholders in a rights issue to subscribe to new shares in proportion to their current stake. In India, these entitlements are credited to demat accounts and can be traded.
terms.formula: Share price − Rights issue price (approximate value)

terms.meaning: An offer to existing shareholders to buy new shares, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they already hold.
Transferring a rights entitlement to another person, either by trading it on the stock exchange or off-market, instead of subscribing to the rights shares oneself.
An individual applying for up to ₹2 lakh in an IPO.
The amount of risk an investor or organisation is willing to take on in pursuit of returns.
How much risk you can and are willing to take, based on your age, income, goals, time horizon and temperament.
The degree of loss or volatility an investor can withstand, financially and emotionally, without abandoning their plan.
The return on an investment considered to carry almost no risk, usually the yield on Indian government Treasury bills or bonds.
SEBI's six-level label of a mutual fund's risk, from Low to Very High, which every fund must show and review each month, next to the risk-o-meter of its benchmark.
A bank's assets adjusted for their riskiness, with riskier loans given higher weights, used to calculate how much capital the bank must keep.
terms.formula: Sum of (Exposure × Risk weight)

terms.meaning: A way of fitting a line that takes the median of the slopes between every pair of points instead of using least squares. A few extreme points barely move it.
terms.formula: Theil-Sen slope = Median of (Yj − Yi) ÷ (Xj − Xi) over all pairs of points

terms.meaning: Returns measured over every window of a fixed length, for example every one-year period ending on each day, instead of over a single start and end date.
Equity in the post-deal company received by a seller or manager in exchange for part of their existing stake, instead of cash.

terms.term: Rotation corners (Ahead and gaining, Ahead but slowing, Behind and slipping, Behind but gaining)
terms.meaning: Where an industry sits on two readings, each measured against the average group: its longer-run return (ahead or behind) and its recent return (gaining or slowing).
A weekly ranking of NSE industry groups by how far they have run ahead of the average group, over several periods, with breadth added.
A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a stock has risen versus fallen over the last 14 days.
Real Time Gross Settlement, an RBI-run system in India that transfers money between banks individually and instantly, mainly for large-value payments.
A software-industry benchmark under which a company's revenue growth rate plus its profit margin, often EBITDA or free cash flow margin, totalling 40% or more is considered healthy.
terms.formula: Revenue growth rate (%) + Profit margin (%)

terms.meaning: Annual revenue projected from a shorter recent period, such as the latest month or quarter multiplied out to a full year.
terms.formula: Recent period revenue × Number of such periods in a year

terms.meaning: Steps that lengthen how long a company's cash lasts, by raising more money or cutting net burn through lower costs or higher revenue.
Residual Value to Paid-In: the current value of a fund's remaining investments divided by the capital limited partners have paid in.
terms.formula: Residual NAV ÷ Paid-in capital

terms.meaning: A common informal name for a SAFE (simple agreement for future equity); despite the name, it is not a debt note and carries no interest or repayment date.
Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
The average time from first contact with a potential customer to a signed deal.
How much new recurring revenue a company generates for each rupee spent on sales and marketing, measured by ratios such as the magic number or new ARR divided by sales and marketing spend.
terms.formula: New ARR ÷ Sales and marketing spend

terms.meaning: How fast revenue and net profit have grown, usually shown for the last year and as 3-year and 5-year CAGRs.
aliases: Gap between sales and profit growth

terms.meaning: Sales growth from stores open for at least a set period, such as a year, excluding new or closed stores.
terms.formula: (Current sales of comparable stores − Prior sales) ÷ Prior sales × 100

terms.meaning: A bank deposit account for individuals that pays interest and allows withdrawals, used for everyday savings and payments.
A company that has moved beyond the startup phase, with a proven business model, and is rapidly growing revenue, customers or headcount.

terms.term: Scenario analysis (bear, base and bull cases)
terms.meaning: Working out a value or result under several sets of assumptions, such as a bear, a base and a bull case, sometimes with a probability for each to give a weighted figure.
terms.formula: Weighted value = Sum of (Case value × Probability)

terms.meaning: FinLit Prism's four bands for a company's score, from strongest to weakest: Strong, Healthy, Average and Weak. The label is always shown next to the number.
A tool that lists every company matching rules you set, such as 'P/E below 20 and ROE above 15%'.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India: the government body that regulates stock markets, brokers, mutual funds, research analysts and investment advisers.
Secured debt that shares the same collateral as senior loans but is repaid only after first-lien lenders, so it carries a higher interest rate.
A buyout in which one private equity fund acquires a portfolio company from another private equity fund.
Money paid to existing shareholders for their shares in a transaction, which changes ownership but brings no new cash into the company.
An existing limited partner's stake in a private equity fund, including its unfunded commitment, that is transferred to another investor on the secondary market.
A transaction in which existing shareholders transfer their shares to new or existing investors; the money goes to the departing shareholders, not the company.
A sector is a broad part of the economy, such as Financial Services or Energy. An industry is a narrower group inside it, such as Private Sector Bank or Refineries & Marketing.
An ETF that follows an index of one sector, such as banks or IT, or one theme, such as defence or manufacturing.
Industries taking turns to lead the market. FinLit measures it against the average group: every NSE industry or sector group with a reading, weighted equally.
Equity funds that invest at least 80% in one sector, such as banking or pharma, or one theme, such as defence, technology or consumption.

terms.term: Sectoral index (Nifty Bank, Nifty IT and others)
terms.meaning: An index that tracks the shares of one sector or theme, such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma or Nifty Auto.
A loan backed by collateral, such as property, machinery or shares, which the lender can claim if the borrower defaults.
The umbrella word for financial instruments that can be bought and sold: shares, bonds, mutual fund units and derivatives.
Temporarily lending securities to another party, usually against collateral and a fee, with the borrower obliged to return the same securities later.

The amount received over the face value when a company issues shares, recorded as a separate reserve; in India its use is restricted to purposes such as issuing bonus shares and writing off issue expenses.
terms.formula: (Issue price − Face value) × Shares issued

terms.meaning: The process of pooling loans or receivables and converting them into tradable securities sold to investors, usually through a special purpose vehicle.
A trust that receives a pool of loans from a lender and issues securities to investors, passing on the collections from those loans.
An instrument issued by an asset reconstruction company to investors, often including the bank that transferred the loans, giving them a share of recoveries from acquired bad loans.
Additional funding raised after a seed round, usually on similar terms, to extend runway before the startup is ready for Series A.
The first sizeable round of outside capital a startup raises, used to build its product, win early customers and prove the idea works.
The assets used by a particular business or geographic segment of a company, disclosed in segment reporting.
terms.formula: Segment return = Segment profit ÷ Segment assets

terms.meaning: The liabilities arising from the operations of a particular business or geographic segment, disclosed in segment reporting.
The breakdown of revenue and profit by business line or region, such as Oil-to-Chemicals, Retail and Digital for Reliance.
A loan from the seller to the acquirer for part of the purchase price, repaid over time with interest.
Operating costs not tied directly to production: marketing, advertising, distribution, sales commissions, office rent, administrative salaries and other corporate overheads.
The loans in a buyout that rank first for repayment and are usually secured on the company's assets, so they carry the lowest interest rate in the debt structure.
A table that shows how a result changes as one or two inputs change, such as the value per share for each pair of discount rate and growth rate.
Growth measured against the immediately preceding period, such as this quarter versus the previous quarter.
terms.formula: (This period − Previous period) ÷ Previous period × 100

terms.meaning: The first major priced venture capital round after seed, typically raised once a startup has a working product and early traction, to scale its business model.
A venture round after Series A, raised to expand a business that has shown its model works, by growing teams, markets and sales.
A later venture round raised by an established startup to scale further, enter new markets, make acquisitions or prepare for an IPO.
A funding round after Series C, raised to keep scaling, extend runway before an IPO, or cover a gap when earlier plans took longer than expected.
A late-stage round after Series D, usually from growth, crossover or private equity investors, for companies staying private longer or needing more capital before an exit.
The part of the total addressable market a company's product can actually serve, given its business model, geography and product scope.
The portion of the serviceable available market a company can realistically capture in the near term, given competition and its resources.
terms.formula: SAM × Achievable market share

terms.meaning: The process of handing over shares and money after a trade. In India most trades settle one working day after the trade date (T+1).
The time between a trade and its settlement, when shares and money actually change hands between the two sides. Indian equities settle on T+1, the next trading day.
A fund maintained by a clearing corporation to complete trades if a clearing member defaults on its obligations, so that counterparties still receive their shares or money.
The amount a company spends on repurchasing its own shares over a year, expressed as a percentage of its market capitalisation.
terms.formula: Net amount spent on share repurchases ÷ Market capitalisation

terms.meaning: The money a company has raised by issuing shares, shown in the balance sheet at face value. Indian companies report authorised, issued and paid-up share capital separately.
terms.formula: Number of shares issued × Face value per share

terms.meaning: The binding contract under which the existing owners of shares transfer them to an acquirer, covering price, conditions, warranties, indemnities and completion mechanics.
Rights giving an investor or shareholder the option to acquire additional shares on agreed terms, such as in future rounds or from other shareholders.
In Indian deals, the agreement under which investors subscribe for new shares issued by a company, usually signed with a shareholders' agreement (SHA) that governs ongoing rights.
An agreement recording the transfer of existing shares from one shareholder to another, setting out the price, number of shares and conditions; the company receives no money.
Compensation paid to employees or others in the form of shares or share options, or cash linked to the share price, expensed at fair value over the vesting period.
terms.formula: Fair value at grant ÷ Vesting period

terms.meaning: A portion reserved for shareholders of a listed parent or group company, usually up to 10% of the issue. Insurers sometimes reserve a policyholder portion in the same way.
The total gain to shareholders from owning a company's shares over a period, combining the change in share price and the dividends received.
terms.formula: (Ending price − Starting price + Dividends) ÷ Starting price

terms.meaning: A contract among a company's shareholders setting out their rights and duties, such as board seats, voting, information rights, transfer restrictions and exit rights.
The quarterly breakdown of who owns a company's shares: promoters, foreign institutions, domestic institutions, government and the public.
The total number of a company's shares currently issued and owned by all shareholders, including promoters and institutions, excluding shares the company has repurchased and cancelled.
Return earned above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility.
terms.formula: Sharpe = (Return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation
aliases: Return for each unit of price swing

terms.meaning: Shares sold in the day without being held, as the exchange reports them from the brokers' disclosures: the share and the quantity, with no client name.
Loans and other debt repayable within 12 months, such as working capital loans, cash credit, overdrafts and commercial paper, plus the current portion of long-term debt in some presentations.
A separate agreement between a general partner and a specific limited partner that changes or adds to the fund's terms for that investor, such as fees, reporting or excuse rights.
A market or stock whose price moves within a fairly stable range for an extended period, without a clear upward or downward trend.
A contract, created by Y Combinator, in which an investor gives a startup money now for the right to receive equity later, usually at the next priced round, with no interest or maturity date.
Interest calculated only on the original principal.
terms.formula: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: Vesting acceleration that happens on one event alone, usually the company's acquisition, whether or not the person keeps their job.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, in a mutual fund.
The share of a bank's standard loans that turned into non-performing assets during a period.
terms.formula: Fresh NPAs during the period ÷ Standard advances at start × 100

terms.meaning: A type of bank licensed by the RBI to take deposits and lend mainly to small businesses, farmers, low-income families and the unorganised sector.
An IPO by a small or medium company that lists on a separate platform, NSE Emerge or BSE SME.
A SEBI category of funds built around a goal, retirement funds and children's funds, with a lock-in of at least five years or until retirement age or the child comes of age, whichever is earlier.
A company's ability to meet all its long-term obligations and keep operating.
A table showing where the money for a deal comes from, such as debt and sponsor equity, and where it goes, such as purchase price, debt refinancing and fees; both sides must match.
terms.formula: Total sources = Total uses

terms.meaning: A bond issued by a national government, in its own or a foreign currency.
A price-discovery session on listing day, when orders are collected and a fair opening price is set before normal trading usually begins at 10 am.
A separate legal entity created for a specific purpose, such as financing a project or keeping securitised assets apart from the parent company's risks.
A chart with one spoke per measure, each running from weaker at the centre to stronger at the edge, joined into a shape. Several companies can be drawn on top of each other.
The equity a private equity firm (the sponsor) invests in a buyout from its fund, as opposed to equity from management or co-investors.

A way of describing where a share is in its price cycle using a long moving average: Stage 1 basing (the average flat), Stage 2 advancing (price above a rising average), Stage 3 topping (flat again after a rise) and Stage 4 declining (price below a falling average).
Financial statements of a single legal entity, excluding the results of its subsidiaries, which appear only as investments.
A measure of how spread out values are around their average. In a roughly bell-shaped spread, about two-thirds of values lie within one standard deviation of the average.
terms.formula: Standard deviation = √(Average of (Value − Mean)²)

terms.meaning: An RBI facility, introduced in 2022, through which banks can deposit surplus funds with the RBI without the RBI giving collateral in return; its rate forms the floor of the policy corridor.
A FinLit flag for a stock at a 1-year high while its industry is still well below its own high. Strong standout: the industry is far below its high. Early standout: the industry is somewhat below it.
A pre-arranged debt package offered by the seller's adviser to all bidders in an auction, which they may use to fund their acquisition.
A fixed-term programme, often three to six months, that gives a cohort of early startups mentoring, networking and usually a small investment for equity, ending in a demo day.

An organisation, often linked to a university, company or government body, that supports very early startups over a longer, open-ended period with workspace, mentoring and services, sometimes for equity or fees.
A statement reconciling shareholders' equity at the start and end of a period, showing profit added, dividends paid, new shares issued, buybacks and other comprehensive income.
terms.formula: Opening equity + Profit + OCI + Shares issued − Dividends − Buybacks = Closing equity

terms.meaning: A statement showing how retained earnings moved over a period: opening balance plus profit, minus dividends and other adjustments. Under Ind AS this appears within the statement of changes in equity.
terms.formula: Opening retained earnings + Net profit − Dividends

terms.meaning: The legally required annual audit of a company's financial statements by an independent external auditor, mandated in India by the Companies Act, 2013.
The share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that it must keep in liquid assets such as cash, gold or approved government securities.
terms.formula: SLR assets ÷ Net demand and time liabilities × 100

terms.meaning: A SIP whose instalment rises each year, by a fixed amount or a percentage, for example in line with pay rises.
terms.formula: Instalment in year n = First instalment × (1 + Step-up %)^(n − 1)

terms.meaning: A small piece of ownership in a company. Owning one share of a company with 100 crore shares means you own one part in 100 crore of it.
A regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade securities. India's two main exchanges are the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange).
India's exchange-based scheme, known as SLB, in which investors lend shares from their demat accounts to borrowers for a fee, with the clearing corporation guaranteeing the return of the shares.
A right, but not an obligation, to acquire a company's shares at a fixed exercise price within a set period; in startups, usually granted to employees.
terms.formula: (Share value − Exercise price) × Number of options

terms.meaning: Dividing each share into smaller units, for example one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares. The price per share falls in proportion.

FinLit's plain names for the four stages of a share's price cycle: Accumulation (moving sideways after a fall), Advancing (above a rising long-term average), Distribution (moving sideways after a rise) and Declining (below a falling long-term average).
Out of every 100 counted stocks in an industry, how many are trading above their medium-term average price. Sector Pulse shows it as a number and draws it as a line over the last 6 months.
An order that sells automatically if the price falls to a level you choose.
A depreciation method that charges an equal amount every year over an asset's useful life.
terms.formula: (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life

terms.meaning: A company, rather than a purely financial investor, that invests in a startup for business reasons such as access to technology, products, partnerships or a possible future acquisition.
The sale of a company or stake to a strategic acquirer, an operating company that wants it for synergies, market share or capabilities rather than purely financial return.
Plain-language findings FinLit draws from a company's numbers, such as 'profit backed by cash' or 'price below its long-term trend'.
The price at which an option lets its buyer buy the underlying (a call) or sell it (a put).
How much demand there was compared with shares on offer. '25 times subscribed' means bids for 25 times the shares available.
A contract under which an investor agrees to subscribe for new shares issued by a company at a set price, setting out the amount, conditions and closing steps.
A short-term credit facility a fund borrows against its investors' uncalled commitments, used to fund deals quickly before calling capital.
A company controlled by another (its parent), usually through owning more than half its shares.
Valuing a company by valuing each business segment or subsidiary separately and adding them up, less net debt.
terms.formula: Sum of segment values − Net debt

terms.meaning: How much a company depends on a few suppliers for key inputs.
terms.formula: Purchases from top suppliers ÷ Total purchases × 100

terms.meaning: The fastest rate a company can grow using only retained earnings, without issuing new shares or changing its debt-to-equity ratio.
terms.formula: ROE × Retention ratio

terms.meaning: Ordinary shares offered to management in a buyout at a low cost, while the sponsor puts most of its money into preference shares or loan notes, giving managers a larger share of upside.
The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, a global secure messaging network banks use to send payment instructions and financial messages.
When the price pushes past a recent swing high or swing low but cannot hold there and closes back inside the earlier range.
The short code a stock trades under, such as RELIANCE on the NSE, and the six-digit number BSE uses, such as 500325.
A large loan provided jointly by a group of lenders, arranged and managed by one or more lead banks, to a single borrower.
A mutual fund facility that redeems a fixed amount or number of units at regular intervals and pays the money to the investor's bank account.
IPO shares must list within three working days after the issue closes (T). Allotment is finalised on T+1, shares are credited and unused money unblocked on T+2, and listing happens on T+3.
A right allowing minority shareholders to join a sale by a majority shareholder, transferring their shares at the same price and on the same terms.
The share of the total transaction value on a marketplace or platform that the company keeps as revenue through commissions and fees.
terms.formula: Platform revenue ÷ GMV × 100

terms.meaning: The acquisition of a listed company's shares by an investor, often a private equity fund, so that the company is delisted from the stock exchange.
Shareholders' equity minus intangible assets such as goodwill, brands and patents: the book value backed by physical and financial assets.
terms.formula: Shareholders' equity − Intangible assets − Goodwill

terms.meaning: The price-to-earnings multiple you assume the shares will trade at at the end of a scenario, used to turn a projected EPS into a price.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Future EPS × Target P/E

terms.meaning: An amount you can subtract from income before tax is calculated, such as Section 80C investments under the old tax regime.
terms.formula: Taxable income = Gross income − Deductions

terms.meaning: The income tax charged in the profit and loss statement for a period, made up of current tax payable for the year and deferred tax arising from timing differences.
terms.formula: Current tax + Deferred tax

terms.meaning: Tax withheld by the payer, such as a company paying dividends or a bank paying interest, and paid to the government on your behalf.
Studying price and trading volume to judge trends and momentum, rather than studying the business itself (fundamental analysis).

FinLit's two price-trend scores: a short-term view of recent weeks and a long-term view of the past year. Trend alignment puts the two together in plain words, such as 'Rising on both', 'Dip in an uptrend' or 'Falling on both'.
A bad loan removed from a bank's books after full provisioning, while the bank still keeps its legal right and efforts to recover the money.
A loan of a fixed amount repaid over a set period, often several years, usually used to fund long-term assets like machinery or buildings.
A senior term loan, usually from banks, repaid in substantial instalments over its life, typically about five to seven years.
A senior term loan, usually placed with institutional investors, with minimal amortisation, often 1% a year, and most principal repaid at maturity.
A short document listing the key terms of a proposed investment, such as valuation, amount, rights and conditions, which forms the basis for the final legal agreements.
In a DCF, the value of all the cash flows after the forecast years, rolled into one figure at the end of the forecast.
terms.formula: Terminal value = Final-year FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)

terms.meaning: A stock index built around a theme, such as consumption, digital, infrastructure or manufacturing, that draws companies from several sectors linked to that theme.
Investing in companies linked to a long-term trend or idea, such as electric vehicles, digitalisation or defence manufacturing, across several sectors.
A bank's core capital, consisting of Common Equity Tier 1 plus Additional Tier 1 instruments such as perpetual bonds, which absorb losses while the bank continues operating.
terms.formula: Tier 1 capital ÷ Risk-weighted assets × 100

terms.meaning: Supplementary bank capital, such as subordinated debt and certain provisions, which absorbs losses mainly if the bank fails.
How long a price or NAV stayed below its previous high before getting back to it, or how long it has been below it so far.
The total annual revenue opportunity available if a product captured 100% of its relevant market.
terms.formula: Number of potential customers × Average annual revenue per customer

terms.meaning: The full gain from an investment: price change plus dividends or interest received.
terms.formula: Total return % = (End value − Start value + Income) ÷ Start value × 100

terms.meaning: The combined return from share price appreciation and dividends over a period, usually assuming dividends are reinvested, and often expressed as an annualised rate.
terms.formula: (Ending price − Starting price + Dividends) ÷ Starting price

terms.meaning: The ratio of a fund's cumulative distributions plus remaining net asset value to the capital limited partners have paid in.
terms.formula: (Cumulative distributions + Residual NAV) ÷ Paid-in capital

terms.meaning: How far an index fund or ETF's returns drift from the returns of the index it follows, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
terms.formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (fund return − index return)
aliases: Tracking error against the price index

terms.meaning: Financing and risk-reduction tools that support domestic and international trade, such as letters of credit, bank guarantees, export credit and bill discounting.
Amounts a company owes suppliers for goods or services received on credit and not yet paid for.
Amounts customers owe a company for goods or services delivered on credit and not yet paid for.
An exit in which a private equity fund's stake in a portfolio company is sold to a company operating in the same or a related industry.

An exchange segment where every trade must be settled by delivery, so shares bought cannot be sold the same day. Stocks under surveillance or with other concerns are moved into it, marked on NSE by series such as BE.

An exchange segment in which every trade must be settled by actual delivery of shares, so intraday positions cannot be squared off or netted. Exchanges move stocks here mainly for surveillance reasons.
Volume multiplied by price: the rupee value of shares traded in a day.

terms.term: Trading charges (brokerage, STT, stamp duty and others)
terms.meaning: The costs of a trade on top of the price: brokerage, securities transaction tax (STT), exchange transaction charges, the SEBI turnover fee, stamp duty, GST on brokerage and charges, and DP charges when shares leave your demat account.
One trading day on the exchange. NSE and BSE equity trading runs from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST on weekdays, after a pre-open session from 9:00 am.
The number of shares or contracts traded in a security during a period, usually a day.
The share price divided by earnings per share actually reported over the last 12 months.
terms.formula: Share price ÷ EPS of the last 12 months

terms.meaning: How much a fund's NAV changed from a date in the past (one month, six months, one year...) up to the latest NAV.
terms.formula:
1-year return = (Latest NAV ÷ NAV one year earlier) − 1
For more than a year: (Latest NAV ÷ Start NAV)^(365 ÷ days between the two NAV dates) − 1

terms.meaning: A fee charged by a private equity firm to a portfolio company for arranging an acquisition or financing, or the advisory fees paid on a deal.
terms.formula: Fee rate × Transaction value

terms.meaning: A clause limiting a shareholder's or partner's ability to transfer its stake without consent, often including rights of first refusal for others.
A short-term Government of India security (91, 182 or 364 days) issued at a discount and repaid at face value.
Managing a company's or bank's cash, liquidity, investments, borrowings and financial risks such as interest rate and currency exposure.
The general direction of prices over time: up, down or sideways.
A straight line drawn on a price chart through two or more highs or lows to mark the direction of a trend.
A list of all ledger account balances at a point in time, with total debits and total credits, prepared to check that the books balance before preparing financial statements.
terms.formula: Total debits = Total credits

terms.meaning: The total of the last four reported quarters, used instead of the last full fiscal year.
Total Value to Paid-In: the sum of distributions and remaining value divided by capital paid in, giving the fund's overall multiple.
terms.formula: (Cumulative distributions + Residual NAV) ÷ Paid-in capital

terms.meaning: The part of a limited partner's commitment that the general partner has not yet drawn down.
terms.formula: Capital commitment − Capital called

terms.meaning: A promise, usually by banks, to buy shares that investors do not take up, so the company raises the planned amount. More broadly, judging and taking on a risk, as in loans or insurance.
Income received before it has been earned, such as interest, rent or fees collected in advance, shown as a liability until the related period passes or service is provided.
Cash received from customers for goods or services not yet delivered, recorded as a liability until the company performs its obligation.
The share of people in the labour force who are looking for work but do not have it. In India it comes from MoSPI's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
terms.formula: Unemployment rate = Unemployed ÷ Labour force × 100

terms.meaning: A privately owned startup valued at US$1 billion or more.
The revenues and costs tied to a single unit of business, such as one customer, order or subscription, used to check whether each unit is profitable.
The revenue and costs tied to a single unit of the business, such as one store, customer, order or product, showing whether each unit is profitable.
A single loan that combines senior and junior debt into one facility with one blended interest rate and one set of documents, usually from a private credit lender.
A bank that offers a full range of services, including deposits, loans, investment banking, insurance distribution and wealth management.
Free cash flow before any interest or debt payments, available to all capital providers.
terms.formula: NOPAT + Depreciation − Capital expenditure − Increase in working capital

terms.meaning: A clean audit opinion stating that the financial statements give a true and fair view in all material respects; now called an unmodified opinion.
The paper profit or loss on an investment you still hold.
terms.formula: Unrealised gain = Current market value − Purchase cost

terms.meaning: The internal rate of return on investments still owned, using their current estimated fair value as if received today.
terms.formula: Discount rate at which NPV of cash flows plus current fair value = 0

terms.meaning: The current estimated fair value of investments a fund still owns and has not yet exited.
A loan with no collateral, such as a personal loan or credit card, given on the basis of your credit history.
A funding round in which a startup issues shares at a higher price per share than in its previous round.
Unified Payments Interface, an NPCI-run instant payment system in India that links bank accounts to mobile apps for transfers using a virtual address or QR code.
The approval request you accept in your UPI app to block IPO money, used for applications up to ₹5 lakh.
Working out what an asset or company is worth, and comparing that with its price.
terms.formula: DCF value = Sum of FCF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t

terms.meaning: The maximum valuation at which a SAFE or convertible note converts into equity, so early investors pay a lower price if the next round is priced higher.
A group within a fund manager, often including people outside the deal team, that reviews and approves the fair values of portfolio investments each period.
A reduction, often 10–25%, in the share price at which a SAFE or convertible note converts, compared with the price paid by new investors in the next round.
terms.formula: Conversion price = Next-round price × (1 − Discount rate)

terms.meaning: A ratio that expresses a company's value relative to a financial measure, such as price to earnings, EV to EBITDA, or price to book.
terms.formula: Value (price or EV) ÷ Financial metric

terms.meaning: A detailed plan, usually drawn up around the deal, setting out how the private equity owner and management will raise a portfolio company's value, with initiatives, timelines and measures.
An investment style that looks for companies trading below their estimated intrinsic value, often identified by low price-to-earnings or price-to-book ratios.
Style buckets for stocks: value stocks trade at low valuations, growth stocks at high valuations backed by fast growth, and blend sits in between.
A cost that rises and falls with how much is produced or sold, such as raw materials or delivery charges.
terms.formula: Total cost = Fixed cost + (Variable cost per unit × Units)

terms.meaning: Funding provided by the seller to help an acquirer pay for a business, such as a seller note or deferred payment.
Money invested in young, fast-growing private companies in exchange for a share of ownership.
Loans to venture-backed startups, usually from specialist lenders and often with warrants attached, used to extend runway with less dilution than raising equity.
A clause that makes unvested shares or options vest earlier than scheduled, usually on events such as an acquisition or termination of employment.
The timetable over which an employee or founder earns the right to shares or options, such as monthly over four years after a one-year cliff.
The year a private equity fund makes its first investment or has its first close, used to group funds that started investing in similar market conditions.
The average number of new users each existing user brings in through invitations or referrals.
terms.formula: Invitations sent per user × Conversion rate of invitations

terms.meaning: How much a price swings up and down, usually measured as the standard deviation of returns and stated per year.
terms.formula: Volatility = Standard deviation of returns

terms.meaning: An index of the market's expected volatility over the next 30 days, derived from option prices. India VIX, computed by NSE from Nifty 50 options, is the Indian benchmark.
A stretch when a share's daily price range narrows well below its usual width. A breakout from a squeeze is the first strong move out of the narrow range.
The number of shares traded in a period, usually a day.

terms.term: Volume profile (value area and point of control)
terms.meaning: A count of how much volume traded at each price over a period. The point of control is the price with the most volume; the value area is the band around it where most of the volume, usually about 70%, traded.
Repayment of a loan earlier than required, at the borrower's choice, sometimes subject to a prepayment fee.
An account a domestic bank keeps for a foreign bank, usually in the domestic currency; 'vostro' means 'yours'.
The blended required return of debt and equity providers, weighted by their share in financing.
terms.formula: WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − Tax rate)

terms.meaning: Your list of stocks to follow, with notes and price targets.
An anti-dilution method that lowers an investor's conversion price to a weighted average of the old price and the down-round price, taking into account how many new shares are issued.
terms.formula: New price = Old price × (A + B) ÷ (A + C), where A = shares before the round, B = new money ÷ old price, C = new shares issued

terms.meaning: The average number of shares outstanding during a period, with each share counted for the part of the period it existed.
terms.formula: Weighted average shares = Σ (shares outstanding × fraction of the period outstanding)

terms.meaning: A borrower who does not repay a loan despite having the ability to, or who diverts or siphons borrowed funds, as classified by lenders under RBI guidelines.
The share of closed trades that ended in a profit.
terms.formula: Win rate % = Winning trades ÷ All closed trades × 100

terms.meaning: Inventory of goods that have entered production but are not yet finished, valued at the cost of materials, labour and overheads incurred so far.
Current assets minus current liabilities; a measure of resources available for day-to-day operations.
terms.formula: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

terms.meaning: Short-term funding that pays for day-to-day needs such as inventory, receivables and supplier payments, through cash credit, overdrafts or bill discounting.
Net working capital as a share of revenue: how much money is tied up in inventory and receivables, less payables, for each rupee of sales.
terms.formula: Net working capital ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: A short-term loan used to finance day-to-day operations such as purchasing raw materials, paying wages and carrying receivables.
Removing an asset, such as a bad loan, from the balance sheet because it is considered unrecoverable, with the loss charged against provisions or profits.
A depreciation method that applies a fixed percentage to the asset's remaining book value each year, so the charge is highest early and declines over time.
terms.formula: Opening book value × Depreciation rate

terms.meaning: eXtensible Business Reporting Language: a standard format for tagging financial statements so computers can read them.
The annualised return for investments made on different dates, such as monthly SIPs.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_i ÷ (1 + XIRR)^((d_i − d_0) ÷ 365)

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the same period a year earlier, such as Jun 2026 quarter against Jun 2025 quarter.
terms.formula: YoY % = (This period − Same period last year) ÷ Same period last year × 100
aliases: Operating profit growth, year on year
Profit growth vs same quarter last year
Sales growth vs same quarter last year

terms.meaning: The income an investment pays each year as a percentage of its price.
terms.formula: Current yield = Yearly income ÷ Current price

terms.meaning: A line showing the yields of bonds of the same credit quality across different maturities, usually based on government securities.
The average interest rate a bank earns on its loans, calculated as interest income from loans divided by average loans outstanding.
terms.formula: Interest income on advances ÷ Average advances × 100

terms.meaning: The annualised return implied by a bond's price, coupons and repayment at maturity, assuming stated cash flows and holding to maturity.
terms.formula: Price = Sum of C ÷ (1 + YTM)^t + Face value ÷ (1 + YTM)^n

terms.meaning: Building each budget from zero, justifying every expense, instead of starting from last year's figures.
A bond that pays no regular interest. It is sold below face value and repays face value at maturity; the difference is your return.
terms.formula: Price = Face value ÷ (1 + r)^n

terms.meaning: A startup that survives, often earning just enough to cover costs, but grows too slowly to raise new funding or deliver a meaningful exit for investors.
